newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian economy slows, rate cut clamour grows.
newsitem.headline: Australian economy slows, rate cut clamour grows.

text.p: Chances of another Australian interest rate cut rose on Wednesday with the release of data showing economic growth slowing and benign inflation.
Official data showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.8 percent in the September quarter, with annual growth slowing to 3.8 percent from above five percent earlier this year.

On the inflation front, the GDP deflator -- a broader based measure of inflation than the consumer price index (CPI) -- fell 0.4 percent in the quarter, to be only 1.3 percent higher over the past year. Over the same period, the CPI rose 2.1 percent.
The combination of a slowing economy and low inflation has led economists to see a possible third cut in official interest rates by early 1997. Offical cash rates are now 6.5 percent.

"With domestic economic growth continuing to ease in late 1996, unemployment stuck above 8.5 percent and underlying inflation and wages pressures continuing to track lower, we believe that another cut in official interest rates is in the pipeline," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
Official cash rates were last cut by 50 percentage points on both July 31 and November 6.
"Although there is a long way to go until February, the odds are increasingly firming for a February rate cut," Societe Generale economists said in a commentary.
It was the patchy nature of the economic performance, and a pleasant surprise on the inflation front, that led to calls for the Reserve Bank of Australia to cut rates in early 1997.
However, some economists saw enough signs of strength in the data to doubt whether another rate cut was needed.
The data, as has been the case in recent times, showed a mixed Australian economy, with some sectors performing strongly while others were struggling.
"Today's national accounts clearly illustrate the dichotomous nature of the Australian economy at present," the Societe Generale economists said.
While business investment remained strong, weakening personal consumption hampered the retail sector, and the public sector made a detraction from growth.

"September quarter GDP provides a strong base for growth in 1996/97," Macqaurie Bank economists said, adding that "with monetary policy now focused on growth, today's data reduces the chance of another official cut in interest rates".

UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts also saw the strength in the data, saying "it is highly likely that annual economic growth has bottomed in the September quarter and will accelerate from here".
"The data tends to confirm why it is unlikely the Reserve Bank will consider further interest rate cuts," he added.

But former Reserve Bank of Australia governor Bernie Fraser disagrees. In an Australian television interview on Tuesday night he said he thought the bank should have cut rates by one percent in November, citing low inflation and sluggish economy.

Fraser's comments saw the Australian dollar suffer its biggest fall in a decade. At Wednesday's local close the dollar was struggling to hold 79.5 U.S. cents after losing almost three cents overnight from a peak of 81 U.S. cents.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello on Wednesday said the GDP data showed the economy continued to grow solidly, led by investment, but also said conditions were mixed across sectors.
"What you're seeing is economic growth being led by investment and that's just what you'd want to see as you look down the track," Costello told reporters.
"We've already reduced official interest rates and that augurs well for continued investment in 1997."
